summary: Josef Maria Abs worked in Indology and philosophy, studying under Hermann Jacobi at the University of Bonn (~1913–1921). He held a professorship at the University of Calcutta in 1914.

Josef Markwart specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, and linguistics. He studied at Tübingen (Ph.D.) and Bonn, and held posts at Tübingen, the National Museum of Ethnology, Leiden, and Humboldt University of Berlin.
Josef Partsch studied at the University of Breslau (~1900–1905). Active in history and archaeology, he held academic positions in Berlin, Geneva, Göttingen, Freiburg, and Bonn.

Josef Schick, a scholar of linguistics, studied at Tübingen and under Albrecht Weber at Humboldt University of Berlin (PhD). He taught at Berlin, Bonn, Heidelberg, and the University of Munich, where he was ordentlicher Professor from 1896 to 1925.

Josef Strzygowski studied at Vienna, Berlin, and Munich (Ph.D.). Specializing in art history and archaeology, he held posts at the University of Vienna, the University of Graz, and Åbo Akademi University.

Josef Zubatý, an Indologist and linguist, earned his Ph.D. at Charles University studying under Alfred Ludwig. He spent his career at Charles University, serving as Privatdozent from 1885 and Professor of Sanskrit and comparative Indo-European from 1894 to 1925.
Josef van Ess worked in religious studies. He studied at the University of Bonn (~1953–1959) and held a post at the University of Tübingen (~1968–1999).
Joseph Ammann was an Indologist who studied under Othmar Frank. In 1836, he served as a teacher at the Hans-Carossa-Gymnasium in Landshut.

Joseph Campbell studied at Canterbury School, Dartmouth, Columbia University (B.A., master's), Paris, and Munich. Working in religious studies, he taught at Canterbury School and was on the faculty of Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972.
Joseph D. Markowski worked in Buddhist studies and Japanology. He earned a Master of Arts at McGill University under the supervision of G. Victor Sōgen Hori (attested 2004).

Joseph Dahlmann was an Indologist who studied under Georg Bühler in Vienna and earned his Ph.D. in Berlin. A founder of Sophia University, he taught there in 1913 and at the University of Tokyo from 1914 to 1924.

Joseph Dalton Hooker earned an M.D. at the University of Glasgow (~1832–1839). He worked at the British Geological Survey (1845–1847) and served as Assistant Director and Director of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (1855–1885).

Joseph David Beglar studied civil engineering at Shibpur and Hooghly Mohsin College. Active in archaeology and Indology, he worked for the Public Works Department in Bengal and the Archaeological Survey of India (1871–1890).

Joseph E. Schwartzberg was a geographer in Indology and history who studied at Brooklyn College, Maryland, the Sorbonne, and Wisconsin-Madison (PhD) under Richard Hartshorne. He taught at Pennsylvania, Jawaharlal Nehru University, and the University of Minnesota (1964–2000).

Joseph Edward Harry studied at Johns Hopkins under Maurice Bloomfield. He held academic posts in classics, Greek, and German at Georgetown College, the University of Cincinnati, the Sorbonne, and Bard College.

Joseph Edward Lyall Brandreth studied at Eton College and the East India Company College. He worked in linguistics and Indology, and served as a Member of the Imperial Legislative Council from 1867 to 1869.

Joseph Estlin Carpenter studied at UCL, London, Oxford, and Zurich. Active in Buddhist studies and religion, he was a professor and principal at Harris Manchester College, Oxford, and Wilde Lecturer in Comparative Religion at Oxford (1914–1924).

Joseph Gabet was active in Tibetology, Sinology, and religious studies. He completed his education at the Petit Séminaire de Vaux-sur-Poligny (~1823–1828) and the Grand Séminaire de Saint-Claude (~1828–1833).

Joseph Goldstein, active in Buddhist studies, studied at Columbia and under teachers including Anagarika Munindra, S. N. Goenka, and Mahasi Sayadaw. He taught at Naropa University in 1974 and co-founded the Insight Meditation Society.

Joseph Hackin studied in Paris under Sylvain Lévi, Louis Finot, Édouard Chavannes, and Paul Pelliot. He was curator at the Guimet Museum, taught at the École du Louvre and EPHE, and directed the DAFA and Maison Franco-Japonaise.
